title: Generators
summary: Run a generator only outside, more than 20 feet (6 m) from windows, doors and vents, with the exhaust pointing away from buildings. Never in the garage, basement or on a porch. Never plug it into a wall outlet: anything wired into the house, like the furnace or well pump, needs a transfer switch put in by an electrician.
doFirst: Run it only outside, more than 20 feet (6 m) from windows, doors and vents, with the exhaust pointing away from the house (CDC, CPSC).
Never in the house, garage, basement, crawlspace, shed, porch or carport, even with doors and windows open (CPSC).
Never plug the generator into a wall outlet. It can feed power back into the lines and kill line workers (University of Illinois Extension, Cornell).
Turn it off and let it cool before you refuel it (OSHA, FEMA).
Keep battery CO alarms working in the house while it runs (CDC).

blocks.warn: A generator’s exhaust is full of carbon monoxide. Opening doors or windows will not let enough air in to stop it building up to deadly levels (CPSC). About 100 people in the US die each year from carbon monoxide from portable generators (CPSC).

list: Outside only, more than 20 feet (6 m) from any window, door or vent (CDC, New York State Division of Consumer Protection). CPSC: at least 20 feet (6 m) from the house.
Point the exhaust away from your home and from any other building someone can go into (CPSC).
Close windows and seal off vent openings near the generator or in the path of its exhaust (CPSC).

Never inside a home, garage, basement, crawlspace or shed, or in any other enclosed or partly enclosed space, even one with some ventilation (CPSC, FEMA). Never in an attached garage, even with the door open (NFPA).
Never on a porch or in a carport (CPSC).
Keep it as far as you can from your home and from your neighbors’ homes (CPSC and US Fire Administration).
Leave 3 to 4 feet (0.9 to 1.2 m) of clear space on all sides and above it (OSHA).
Keep children and pets away. Parts get hot enough to burn you while it runs (University of Illinois Extension).

blocks.cap: Outside only, more than 20 feet (6 m) from any window, door or vent, with the exhaust pointed away from your home. Never in an attached garage, even with the door open.

blocks.p: When you buy one, look for a generator with a CO shut-off that turns it off automatically (CPSC).

blocks.label: Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors

list: Keep it dry: a wet generator can give you an electric shock (OSHA, Cornell, University of Illinois Extension).

OSHA says not to run it in the rain or wet conditions. If you must run it in wet weather anyway, use it only when you have to, and run it under an open, canopy-like cover, on a dry surface where water can’t puddle or run under it (University of Illinois Extension). Put it where rain and snow can’t reach it, if you can (New York State Division of Consumer Protection).
The cover must stay open. A shed, garage, porch or carport is not a cover: carbon monoxide builds up in partly enclosed spaces (CPSC, FEMA).
Dry your hands before you touch it (University of Illinois Extension).
Follow the maker’s instructions about electric shock in bad weather (CPSC).

blocks.warn: Never plug a generator into a wall outlet. Power can flow back through the house wiring onto the utility lines and kill or injure line workers who think the line is dead (Cornell, University of Illinois Extension).

list: Never attach a generator to the house’s electrical system without a properly installed transfer switch (OSHA).

A qualified electrician should install the generator and the transfer switch (University of Illinois Extension, OSHA, NFPA). The switch keeps the generator’s power from going back onto the utility lines (University of Illinois Extension).
Make sure the transfer switch is in the generator (auxiliary) position before you start the generator (Cornell).

blocks.p: To run the furnace or a well pump from a generator, have a qualified electrician install a transfer switch, so the generator can feed the house wiring safely (University of Illinois Extension; OSHA: never attach a generator to a building’s electrical system without one).

list: Size: Cornell Cooperative Extension says a 4,000 to 6,000 watt portable generator is enough for pumping water, running the furnace, a refrigerator and a few lights. Keeping close to normal living takes 12,000 to 15,000 watts (Cornell).
Choosing one: ask a qualified dealer or electrician which generator suits your house (University of Illinois Extension). Ratings differ between makers, so check what a rating means (Cornell).
Motors take 3 to 5 times as much current to start as to run (Cornell).
Decide ahead which circuits you really need in a long outage (Cornell).

steps: Start the generator with nothing plugged in (Cornell, University of Illinois Extension).
Plug appliances straight into the generator, or into a heavy-duty, outdoor-rated extension cord (NFPA, University of Illinois Extension).
Turn appliances and lights on one at a time, so you don’t overload it (University of Illinois Extension). Start the largest loads first (Cornell).
Never overload it: that can overheat it and start a fire (OSHA, Cornell).
Before you shut it off, switch off everything on it and let it run a few minutes with no load (Cornell).

list: Use cords rated, in watts or amps, for what they carry. Replace an underrated cord with one that has heavier-gauge wire (OSHA).
Check cords for cuts, tears and wear, and make sure the plug has all three prongs, including the grounding pin (NFPA). Never use a frayed or damaged cord (OSHA).
If a cord gets hot, replace it with a heavier one (Cornell).
Lay and fasten cords so nobody trips on them (Cornell).
Make sure the generator is properly grounded and the grounding connections are tight (OSHA).

blocks.p: New York State Department of Health: running a generator outdoors for heat is a better option than a kerosene or unvented gas heater during power failures.

list: Only through a transfer switch, so the heater plugs straight into a wall outlet. Never through an extension cord or power strip (US Fire Administration; CPSC: wall outlet, never a power strip).
Plug nothing else into the circuit the heater is on: it can overheat (US Fire Administration).
Never run a heater’s cord under a rug or carpet (CPSC).

Keep everything that can burn at least 3 feet (1 m) from the heater (CPSC, US Fire Administration). Set it on a stable, level surface where it won’t be knocked over (CPSC). Buy one with a tip-over switch (US Department of Energy).
Turn it off when you leave the room or go to bed (US Fire Administration).
Turn it on by itself, like any other appliance: one at a time (University of Illinois Extension).

steps: Turn the generator off (OSHA, FEMA). Never refuel it while it runs (Cornell).
Let it cool down (OSHA, FEMA, NFPA). Fuel spilled on hot engine parts can catch fire (FEMA).
Fill it, then check the oil and other fluids and look for fuel leaks (Cornell).

list: Fuel vapor you can’t see can travel along the ground and be lit by a pilot light or a spark from a switch (FEMA).
Store fuel in a container made and labelled for it, away from the generator and outside where people live, never in the house (NFPA, OSHA, Cornell). See Store fuel safely.
Keep the generator’s tank filled when it is put away, so it starts when you need it (Cornell).
Generators are for temporary use; decide what you need most (University of Illinois Extension).
Most household generators are not built to run nonstop for days (Cornell).

In an outage longer than 8 hours, shut it down two or three times a day to check fluids and let it cool (Cornell). Cornell’s list also says to shut it down at least once every 24 hours; two or three times a day meets both.
Have it inspected every year and replace worn parts (FEMA). Read and follow its manual (CPSC, University of Illinois Extension).

blocks.p: No source opened gives how much fuel a generator burns per hour. Check your generator’s manual.
